title: Penguin Poop is Melting Antarctic Snow - Nautilus
gist: A study in the Journal of Geophysical Research Biogeosciences finds penguin guano on the West Antarctic Peninsula supplies phosphate that fuels green snow algae, which grow on the snow surface; red algae, by contrast, are phosphate-poor and use red pigments as sunscreen when dormant.

insights.claim: A new study in the Journal of Geophysical Research Biogeosciences found that penguin guano has far-reaching effects on the Antarctic landscape by nourishing snow algae growing on the surface.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Biological feedbacks can alter polar surface conditions in ways climate models may underweight.

insights.claim: Green snow algae samples from the West Antarctic Peninsula were richer in phosphate derived from penguin guano, which lets the algae load cells with chlorophyll and boost photosynthesis.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Nutrient availability, not just temperature, governs algal blooms on polar snow.

insights.claim: Red snow algae were low in phosphate and get their color from red pigments that act as sunscreen when the algae go inactive during nutrient scarcity.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Algal color signals nutrient state, potentially useful as a remote-sensing indicator.

insights.claim: The article's headline frames the guano-fed algae as melting Antarctic snow.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Darkened algae-covered snow may accelerate local melt, a second-order climate feedback.

insights.claim: Penguin guano piles are dense enough to show up on satellite images, and staining spreads beyond defecation sites as penguins track it across the snow.
